title: BIOSTAT 718 - Homework Assignment 1
text:
Find a published scientific article of interest to you that exhibits correlated data. Read the article andanswer the following questions.

I chose to evaluate the article, “Repeated cold-water immersion improves autonomic cardiac modulation following five sessions of high-intensity interval exercise” by Malta et al. [1].


What was the primary scientific question?

Does repeated cold-water immersion improve physical recovery following high-intensity interval training (HIIT) in healthy men compared to no cold-water immersion?

What was the study design? Did it involve random sampling from a population, cluster sampling, no sampling? Were repeated measurements taken on individual subjects? What feature(s) of the study design resulted in correlated data?

Study design: Randomized controlled trial. 11 participants were randomly assigned to the treatment arm (cold-water immersion following exercise), while 10 were randomly assigned to the control arm (passive recovery at room temperature).
Sampling: 21 healthy and moderately active men were sampled from the population. There was no cluster sampling, and all 21 participants were independent of each other.
Repeated measures: Yes, repeated measures were taken on individual subjects. Each participant visited a laboratory eight times over a three-week period. The first and second visits were to inform subjects of the study procedures and to collect baseline measurements for resting heart-rate variability (HRV), countermovement jumps (CMJ), various blood markers associated with muscle health. Visits 3-8 were to collect repeated measures for CMJ and resting HRV, followed by a session of HIIT. The 8th visit also included a final blood sample to evaluate the biomarkers at the end of the study. Thus, the only repeated measures were HRV and CMJ for visits 2-8 (baseline to end of study).
Correlated features: The outcome measurements related to post-exercise recovery (HRV and CMJ) were correlated at the participant level. That is to say that paricipant i’s measurements for HRV and CMJ across all time points were correlated with one another.

Name the primary outcome variable? What type of outcome is it? (binary, ordinal, …)

The investigators measured the following co-primary outcomes:

HRV: This is a continuous variable representing the variability in heart rate.
CMJ: Although this is still a little fuzzy to me, my take-away is that this is a continuous variable measured using an algorithm built by the researchers. As participants jumped on a steel plate, various measurements were taken (e.g. force, jump height etc.), and these are what constitue the CMJ
Biomarkers:

CK: Creatinine kinase is a continuous measurement of a biomarker assoicated with muscle stress
LDH: Lactate dehydrogenage is also a continuous measurement associated with muscle stress

Perceived Internal Load: A 10-point scale labeling a participant’s perceived exertion during the exercise session was recorded by the participant at the end of each visit. This “number” was multiplied by the number of minutes spent during the exercise session to create a continuous outcome representing perceived load. However, I will note that I have some personal reservations as to the efficacy of this conversion of an ordinal or latent variable to a continuous outcome.


What is the primary sampling unit (psu)? How many are there? Were all the psu’s observed or did some have missing data?

The primary sampling unit (PSU) was the participant.
There were 21 participants in all.
There is no mention of missing data or dropout, so I assume all PSUs were observed.

What were the elementary units (eu) or sub-units? How many are there in total?

The EU was the laboratory visit number from 2-8. There were 7 repeated measures.

Is the number of units the same in each cluster (i.e., ni = n) without accounting for missing responses? If missing responses are accounted for?

Yes, the number of units is the same in each cluster (i.e. for each participants). All participants were measured 7 times with no missing responses.

Did the authors state the magnitude of the within-cluster correlation (ρ)? If yes, what is it? If not, what value would you guess for ρ? Why? Is it reasonable that the correlation would be positive or negative?

The authors did not give the within-cluster correlation (\(\rho\)). However, it seems reasonable that a participant’s performance would hold relatively stable over such a short period (three weeks). For that reason, I assume that the correlation is very high, likely above 0.9. I would only expect a positive correlation.

How did the correlation arise? What mechanism do you think caused the correlation?

The correlation arises because a participant is likely to perform at a similar level to his previous performance. There will probably be some variability, but I expect the within-group variability to be much smaller than the between-group variability.

Name one factor of interest to the investigators. (You can choose a treatment factor or a covariate.) Does this factor characterize units with the cluster or does it characterize an entire cluster (i.e., all the objects within a cluster have the same value of the factor)?

The treatment factor is cold-water immersion (CWI). For each participant, this was identical across all elementary units (lab visits), so this characterizes an entire “cluster.”

State the population characteristic of primary interest to the investigators (e.g., mean, prevalence, odds ratio, etc.)

The researchers were primarily interested in the mean values of each of the continuous co-primary outcomes listed above (HRV, CMJ, CK, LDH, perceived internal load).

Name the primary analysis reported in the paper. Did this analysis account for the correlation in the outcomes?

The statistical analyses section states that the authors used a mixed linear model for each of the repeated endpoints (HRV, CMJ, internal load) considering time (i.e. visits) and groups (CWI and control) as fixed effects and subjects as random effects. In this case, the analysis does account for the correlation of each outcome.

Were there any points regarding the design or analysis that were obscure to you?

I excluded a portion of the paper that spoke of measuring participants’ oxygen intake. This didn’t seem to resolve into any of the reported outcomes.
I am still unsure as to how CMJ was recorded. I assume all metrics (force, jump height etc.) were pooled into a single metric, but this is unclear from the paper.
I mentioned this previously, but the creation of the “perceived internal load” seems suspect to me. I would have preferred this to be handled as a latent outcome with some sort of ordinal regression involved.

title: BIOSTAT 718 - Homework Assignment 1
text:
Part 2
Consider the variance inflation factor: VIF = 1 + (n-1) ρ. (See Lecture Notes 2.)

For what value of ρ is VIF largest? For this value of ρ, what is the value of VIF, and what, therefore, is the variance of \(\bar{Y_i}\)? What, then is the “effective sample size,” i.e., the sample size for uncorrelated outcomes that would give the same value for the variance?


We can see that higher values of \(\rho\) lead to a higher VIF. The range for \(\rho\) is \(-1 \le \rho \le 1\), which means a value of 1 yields the highest VIF. Let’s calculate the VIF when \(\rho = 1\):

\[\begin{align*}
VIF &= 1 + (n - 1)\rho\\
&= 1 + (n - 1)(1)\\
&= 1 - 1 + n\\
&= n
\end{align*}\]

The variance of \(\bar{Y_i}\) is calculated as follows:

\[\begin{align*}
Var(\bar{Y_i}) &= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}VIF\\
&= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}n\\
&= \sigma^2\\
\implies Var(\bar{Y_i}) &= Var(Y_i)
\end{align*}\]

I believe that the “effective sample size” is the number of clusters required to yield the same variance as \(Var(\bar{Y_i})\). Since \(Var(\bar{Y_i}) = Var(Y_i) = \sigma^2\), I believe the effective sample size is 1.


For what value of ρ is VIF equal to 1? For this situation, what is the variance of \(\bar{Y_i}\)? What is the “effective sample size” here? For what value of ρ is VIF less than 1? What is the minimum value of VIF? (Hint: What is the minimum value of the variance of the cluster means?)


When \(\rho = 0\) (i.e. no correlation), \(VIF = 1\).

section: Batch effect: a common technical effect
text:
Batch effect: a common technical effect

In gene expression data, batch effect is a huge problem. In a nutshell, there’s typically a high correlation between sequence data collected on the same day

Some reasons:

Different machines used on different days
Different ways of preparing samples for analysis

How to mitigate this:

Make sure you sample from your exposure of interest and your reference group on the same day

This is a problem for any type of high-throughput sequencing data

title: Week 2: January 17, 2025
section: Goal of data processing in scRNA-seq
text:
Goal of data processing in scRNA-seq

To obtain: (1) a properly normalized and transformed gene expression matrix for future use, and (2) the cell types of each cell or continuous trajectories of cells
Differences across cell types dominate the variance in the data
After identifying cell types, it becomes easier to decompose the observed data into variance across cell types and variance within each cell type
This can be thought of as a hierarchical model: first, the cell type of a cel is determined, and then variations are added to the cell based on the state

Example:

Step 1: Decide the cell type (e.g. immune cell, cancer cell, epithelial cell etc.)
Step 2: Decide the state within a cell type (e.g. activated immune cell vs. quiescent immune cell)
There is much more variance between cell type compared to cell state. When you add these variances, you get the observed data

Seurat loading data
We start by reading in hte data. The Read10X() function reads in the output of the cellaranger pipeline from 10x, returning a unique molecular identified (UMI) count matrix. The values in this matrix represent the number of molecules for each feature (i.e. gene; row) that are detected in each cell (column). Note that more recent versions of cellranger now also output using the h5 file format, which can be read in using th Read10X_h5() function in Seurat.
We next use the count matrix to create a Seurat object. The object serves as a container that contains both data (like the count matrix) and analysis (like PCA, or clustering results) for a single-cell dataset. title: Week 2: January 13
text:
Benefits of longitudinal data analysis

Longitudinal study: subjects are usually measured repeatedly over time
Cross-section (independent data) study: a single outcome is measured for each subject
In longitudinal data analysis (LDA), we can investigate:

Temporal changes within individuals (age effects)
Differences between subjects in tehir baseline levels (cohort effects)
With independent data, we can only investigate cohort effects, ageing effects are not separately identifiable

LDA requires special statistical methods because observations tend to be correlated within individuals

Methods you have probably learned (until today) were for independent data

Why longitudinal data analysis methods?

The repeated observations on a subject, (\(Y_i1,, Y_i2, .., y_in\)) are very likely to be correlated

The assumption of independent observations will be violated

Using (independent data) regression techniques may have problems

Precision estimates (standard errors) will be biased
Mean parameters will often be inefficiently estimated
Inference (tests) will be incorrect
Correlation may be of scientific interest (and will be ignored)

Note: a sample unit or cluster is something like a family, a school, a hospital etc. that is a cluster of observations

title: Week 2: January 13
text:
Ignoring Correlation

Question: What are the effects?

On estimated means, rates (prevalence, incidence), regression coefficients or the precision of the estimates?
Estimated means: none. Why?

Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the outcome on the \(j_{th}\) unit in the \(i_{th}\) cluster. Let I be the total number of clusters. Assume all clusters have the same number of units (\(n_1 = n_2 = ... = n_I = n\)), all observations within a cluster have the same mean, \(E[Y_{ij}] - \mu_i\) and there is a common variance among all observations, \(V[Y_{ij}] = \sigma^2\).
Stuff happens. Turns out the estimators for \(\beta\) are unbiased.

Estimated variance (precision).

Math happens. Turns out that \(V[\bar{Y_i}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\times\left[1 + \rho(n - 1)\right]\). The right-hand side of this is the variance inflation factor.

title: BIOSTAT 718 - Homework 2
text:
Crouse (Am J Cardiol, 2001) noted that intima-media thickness (IMT) of the carotid arteries is a generalized index of atherosclerotic disease. Previous investigators (Spence JD, Am J Cardiol 2002; Folsom AR, Stroke 1993; Howard G, Stroke 1993) have reported that IMT ranges between 0.5 to 1 mm in the general population and increases approximately 0.010 to 0.018 mm/year. Higher values of IMT are associated with more diseased arteries and cardiovascular events. These investigators and others have noted that lifestyle changes or medications may slow, arrest or induce regression in IMT. An investigation of an experimental statin – a medication for individuals at high risk of having cardiovascular disease events (e.g., myocardial infarction, stroke) – was conducted to evaluate the effect of the drug on intima-media thickness (IMT) of the carotid arteries over a one-year period. In the prospective interventional study, approximately 2000 older patients (ages between 65-95 years) were randomized equally in a blinded fashion to receive either 40 mg of an experimental statin or a placebo. Treatments were administered daily for a year.
The intima-media thickness (IMT) of the common carotid arteries were measured by ultrasonography and were collected at two times for the study: prior to the drug or placebo administration (Year 0), and one year later (Year 1).

The dataset is formatted with one record per patient. There are no missing values.

title: BIOSTAT 724 - Homework 1
text:
In answering a question on a multiple-choice test, a student either knows the answer or guesses. Let p be the probability that the student knows the answer and 1- p the probability that the student guesses. Assume that a student who guesses at the answer will be correct with probability 1/m, where m is the number of multiple-choice alternatives. What is the conditional probability that a student knew the answer to a question, given that he or she answered it correctly? What happens when m is very large? What happens when p is close to 0?

Let’s solve this using Baye’s Theorem. First, it’ll be helpful to define some terms:

\(P(\text{Knows}) = p\)
\(P(\text{Guess}) - 1 - p\)
\(P(\text{Correct | Guess}) = \frac{1}{m}\)
We want to know \(P(\text{Knows | Correct})\)


\[\begin{align*}
P(\text{Knows | Correct}) &= \frac{P(\text{Correct | Knows})P(\text{Knows})}{P(\text{Correct | Knows})P(\text{Knows}) + P(\text{Correct | Guess})P(\text{Guess})}\\
&= \frac{(1)(p)}{(1)(p) + (\frac{1}{m})(1 - p)}\\
&= \frac{p}{p + \frac{1 - p}{m}}\\
\end{align*}\]

We can see from this result that as m gets arbitrarily large, the denominator approaches p and the probability goes to 1. This aligns with our intuition because a correct guess among a larger number of choices would be less likely. Likewise, if p is close to 0, the probability is also close to zero.

Problem 2
Suppose urn H is filled with 40% green balls and 60% red balls, and urn T is filled with 60% green balls and 40% red balls. Someone will flip a coin and then select a ball from urn H or urn T depending on whether the coin lands heads or tails, respectively. Let X be 1 or 0 if the coin lands heads or tails, and let Y be 1 or 0 if the ball is green or red.

Part a
Write out the joint distribution of X and Y in a table.

# | echo: false
import pandas as pd

# Define the joint probability table
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {0: [0.2, 0.3], 1: [0.3, 0.2]},
    index=pd.Index([0, 1], name="Y"),
    columns=pd.Index([0, 1], name="X"),
)

# Add marginal probabilities
df["P(Y)"] = df.sum(axis=1)  # Row sums (marginal P(Y))
df.loc["P(X)"] = df.sum(axis=0)  # Column sums (marginal P(X))

# Display the table
print(df)

Y                   
0     0.2  0.3   0.5
1     0.3  0.2   0.5
P(X)  0.5  0.5   1.0




Part b
Find E(Y). What is the probability that the ball is green?
\(E(Y) = \sum y\cdot f_Y(y)\). In our table, we see that Y can take on two values, 0 and 1. We can use the marginal probability to find that \(\sum y\cdot f_Y(y) = (0)(0.5) + (1)(0.5) = 0.5\). Thus, \(P(\text{Ball is green}) = 0.5\).


Part c
Find Var(Y|X=0), Var(Y|X=1) and Var(Y). Thinking of variance as measuring uncertainty, explain intuitively why one of these variances is larger than the others.

Intuitively, I would expect the variance of Y without any additional information regarding X to be greater than either variances of Y given X = 0 and X = 1. That is, I expect \(max(Var(Y), Var(Y|X=0), Var(Y|X=1)) = Var(Y)\). My reasoning is that knowing something about X reduces our uncertainty of Y. Let’s see if I’m correct.

\[
\begin{align*}
Var(Y) &= \sum_{i = 1}^n (Y_i - E[Y])^2\cdot f(Y)\\
&= (0 -0.5)^2(0.5) + (1-0.5)^2(0.5)\\
&= 0.25\\
Var(Y|X=x) &= \sum_{i =1}^n (Y_i - E[Y | x])^2\cdot f(y|x)\\
E(Y|X=x) &= \sum_{i = 1}^nY_i\cdot f(y|x)\\
E(Y|X=0) &= (0)(0.4) + (1)(0.6)\\
&= 0.6\\
E(Y|X=1) &= (0)(0.6) + (1)(0.4)\\
&= 0.4\\
Var(Y|X=0) &= (0 - 0.6)^2(0.4) + (1 - 0.6)^2(0.6)\\
&= 0.24\\
Var(Y|X=1) &= (0 - 0.4)^2(0.6) + (1 - 0.4)^2(0.4)\\
&= 0.24\\
\end{align*}
\]

As I guessed, knowing something about X does reduce the uncertainty around Y. We see that the conditional variances are both less than the variance of Y, even if it is by a small amount.



Part d
Suppose you see that the ball is green. What is the probability that the coin turned up tails?

Let’s solve this in terms of X and Y. Thus, we want \(P(X=0|Y=1)\), which is easily solved using Bayes’ Theorem:

\[\begin{align*}
P(X=0|Y=1) &= \frac{P(Y=1|X=0)P(X=0)}{P(Y=1|X=0)P(X=0) + P(Y=1|X=1)P(X=1)}\\
&= \frac{(0.6)(0.5)}{(0.6)(0.5) + (0.4)(0.5)}\\
&= 0.6
\end{align*}\]

Problem 3
Let \(\theta\) be a Beta(a,b) random variable, and suppose that the conditional distribution of X, given that \(\theta\), is Binomial(n, \(\theta\)). Find the (marginal) probability mass function of X.

We can solve this by integrating out \(\theta\) from the joint distribution.

\[\begin{align*}
f_X(X) &= \int P(X=x|\theta)P(\theta)d\theta\\
&= \int {n \choose x} \theta^x(1 - \theta)^{n - x}\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\frac{\Gamma(a + \beta)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}d\theta\\
&= \int {n \choose x} \theta^{x+a-1}(1 - \theta)^{n + b- x-1}\frac{\Gamma(a + \beta)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}d\theta\\
&= {n \choose x}\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \int\theta^{x+a-1}(1 - \theta)^{n + b- x-1}d\theta\\
&= {n \choose x}\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\frac{\Gamma(x + a - 1)\Gamma(b + n - x - 1)}{\Gamma(a + b + n - 2)}\int \theta^{x+a-1}(1 - \theta)^{n + b- x-1}d\theta \frac{\Gamma(a + b + n - 2)}{\Gamma(x + a - 1)\Gamma(b + n - x - 1)}d\theta\\
&= {n \choose x}\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\frac{\Gamma(x + a - 1)\Gamma(b + n - x - 1)}{\Gamma(a + b + n - 2)} (1)\\
\end{align*}\]

title: BIOSTAT 724 - Homework 1
text:
Problem 4
Full conditionals: Let X,Y,Z be random variables with joint density (discrete or continuous) p(x, y, z) ∝ f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z). Show that

p(x|y, z) ∝ f(x, z), i.e. , p(x|y, z) is a function of x and z;
p(y|x, z) g(y, z), i.e., p(y|x, z) is a function of y and z;
X and Y are conditionally independent given Z.


Part a
\[\begin{align*}
p(x|y, z) &= \frac{p(x, y, z)}{p(y)p(z)}\\
\implies p(x|y, z) &\propto p(x, y, z)\\
\implies p(x|y, z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Note that the only part of this that depends on X is \(f(x, z)\), which implies that \(p(x|y, z) \propto f(x, z)\).



Part b

Let’s solve this in the exact same way.

\[\begin{align*}
p(y|x, z) &= \frac{p(x, y, z)}{p(x)p(z)}\\
\implies p(y|x, z) &\propto p(x, y, z)\\
\implies p(y|x, z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Similarly, the only portion of \(f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\) that depends on y is the term \(g(y, z)\). Thus, \(p(y|x, z) \propto g(y, z)\).



Part c

To be conditionally independent, we need to show that \(p(x, y|z) \propto p(x|z)p(y|z)\).
Let’s begin with the same approach that we followed in parts a and b. We’ll obviously need to get a little fancier for this part, but let’s first show that $p(x, y|z) f(x,z)g(y,z):

\[\begin{align*}
p(y, x| z) &= \frac{p(x, y, z)}{p(z)}\\
\implies p(y,x| z) &\propto p(x, y, z)\\
\implies p(y,x| z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\\
\implies p(y,x| z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Next, we need to think about \(p(x|z)\) and \(p(y|z)\).

\[\begin{align*}
p(x|z) &= \frac{p(x,z)}{p(z)}\\
p(x,z) \propto f(x,z)f(z)\\
\implies p(x|z)\propto f(x,z)\\
p(y|z) &= \frac{p(y,z)}{p(z)}\\
p(y,z) \propto g(y,z)f(z)\\
\implies p(y|z)\propto g(y,z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Combining these results, we see that \(p(x, y | z)\propto f(x,z)g(y,z)\implies p(x, y |z) \propto p(x|z)p(y|z)\). Thus, x and y are conditionally independent.

In answering a question on a multiple-choice test, a student either knows the answer or guesses. Let p be the probability that the student knows the answer and 1- p the probability that the student guesses. Assume that a student who guesses at the answer will be correct with probability 1/m, where m is the number of multiple-choice alternatives. What is the conditional probability that a student knew the answer to a question, given that he or she answered it correctly? What happens when m is very large? What happens when p is close to 0?

Let’s solve this using Baye’s Theorem. First, it’ll be helpful to define some terms:

\(P(\text{Knows}) = p\)
\(P(\text{Guess}) - 1 - p\)
\(P(\text{Correct | Guess}) = \frac{1}{m}\)
We want to know \(P(\text{Knows | Correct})\)


\[\begin{align*}
P(\text{Knows | Correct}) &= \frac{P(\text{Correct | Knows})P(\text{Knows})}{P(\text{Correct | Knows})P(\text{Knows}) + P(\text{Correct | Guess})P(\text{Guess})}\\
&= \frac{(1)(p)}{(1)(p) + (\frac{1}{m})(1 - p)}\\
&= \frac{p}{p + \frac{1 - p}{m}}\\
\end{align*}\]

We can see from this result that as m gets arbitrarily large, the denominator approaches p and the probability goes to 1. This aligns with our intuition because a correct guess among a larger number of choices would be less likely. Likewise, if p is close to 0, the probability is also close to zero.

Problem 2
Suppose urn H is filled with 40% green balls and 60% red balls, and urn T is filled with 60% green balls and 40% red balls. Someone will flip a coin and then select a ball from urn H or urn T depending on whether the coin lands heads or tails, respectively. Let X be 1 or 0 if the coin lands heads or tails, and let Y be 1 or 0 if the ball is green or red.

Part a
Write out the joint distribution of X and Y in a table.

# | echo: false
import pandas as pd

# Define the joint probability table
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {0: [0.2, 0.3], 1: [0.3, 0.2]},
    index=pd.Index([0, 1], name="Y"),
    columns=pd.Index([0, 1], name="X"),
)

# Add marginal probabilities
df["P(Y)"] = df.sum(axis=1)  # Row sums (marginal P(Y))
df.loc["P(X)"] = df.sum(axis=0)  # Column sums (marginal P(X))

# Display the table
print(df)

X       0    1  P(Y)
Y                   
0     0.2  0.3   0.5
1     0.3  0.2   0.5
P(X)  0.5  0.5   1.0




Part b
Find E(Y). What is the probability that the ball is green?
\(E(Y) = \sum y\cdot f_Y(y)\). In our table, we see that Y can take on two values, 0 and 1. We can use the marginal probability to find that \(\sum y\cdot f_Y(y) = (0)(0.5) + (1)(0.5) = 0.5\). Thus, \(P(\text{Ball is green}) = 0.5\).


Part c
Find Var(Y|X=0), Var(Y|X=1) and Var(Y). Thinking of variance as measuring uncertainty, explain intuitively why one of these variances is larger than the others.

Intuitively, I would expect the variance of Y without any additional information regarding X to be greater than either variances of Y given X = 0 and X = 1. That is, I expect \(max(Var(Y), Var(Y|X=0), Var(Y|X=1)) = Var(Y)\). My reasoning is that knowing something about X reduces our uncertainty of Y. Let’s see if I’m correct.

\[
\begin{align*}
Var(Y) &= \sum_{i = 1}^n (Y_i - E[Y])^2\cdot f(Y)\\
&= (0 -0.5)^2(0.5) + (1-0.5)^2(0.5)\\
&= 0.25\\
Var(Y|X=x) &= \sum_{i =1}^n (Y_i - E[Y | x])^2\cdot f(y|x)\\
E(Y|X=x) &= \sum_{i = 1}^nY_i\cdot f(y|x)\\
E(Y|X=0) &= (0)(0.4) + (1)(0.6)\\
&= 0.6\\
E(Y|X=1) &= (0)(0.6) + (1)(0.4)\\
&= 0.4\\
Var(Y|X=0) &= (0 - 0.6)^2(0.4) + (1 - 0.6)^2(0.6)\\
&= 0.24\\
Var(Y|X=1) &= (0 - 0.4)^2(0.6) + (1 - 0.4)^2(0.4)\\
&= 0.24\\
\end{align*}
\]

As I guessed, knowing something about X does reduce the uncertainty around Y. We see that the conditional variances are both less than the variance of Y, even if it is by a small amount.



Part d
Suppose you see that the ball is green. What is the probability that the coin turned up tails?

Let’s solve this in terms of X and Y. Thus, we want \(P(X=0|Y=1)\), which is easily solved using Bayes’ Theorem:

\[\begin{align*}
P(X=0|Y=1) &= \frac{P(Y=1|X=0)P(X=0)}{P(Y=1|X=0)P(X=0) + P(Y=1|X=1)P(X=1)}\\
&= \frac{(0.6)(0.5)}{(0.6)(0.5) + (0.4)(0.5)}\\
&= 0.6
\end{align*}\]

Problem 3
Let \(\theta\) be a Beta(a,b) random variable, and suppose that the conditional distribution of X, given that \(\theta\), is Binomial(n, \(\theta\)). Find the (marginal) probability mass function of X.

We can solve this by integrating out \(\theta\) from the joint distribution.

\[\begin{align*}
f_X(X) &= \int P(X=x|\theta)P(\theta)d\theta\\
&= \int {n \choose x} \theta^x(1 - \theta)^{n - x}\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\frac{\Gamma(a + \beta)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}d\theta\\
&= \int {n \choose x} \theta^{x+a-1}(1 - \theta)^{n + b- x-1}\frac{\Gamma(a + \beta)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}d\theta\\
&= {n \choose x}\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \int\theta^{x+a-1}(1 - \theta)^{n + b- x-1}d\theta\\
&= {n \choose x}\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\frac{\Gamma(x + a - 1)\Gamma(b + n - x - 1)}{\Gamma(a + b + n - 2)}\int \theta^{x+a-1}(1 - \theta)^{n + b- x-1}d\theta \frac{\Gamma(a + b + n - 2)}{\Gamma(x + a - 1)\Gamma(b + n - x - 1)}d\theta\\
&= {n \choose x}\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\frac{\Gamma(x + a - 1)\Gamma(b + n - x - 1)}{\Gamma(a + b + n - 2)} (1)\\
\end{align*}\]

Problem 4
Full conditionals: Let X,Y,Z be random variables with joint density (discrete or continuous) p(x, y, z) ∝ f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z). Show that

p(x|y, z) ∝ f(x, z), i.e. , p(x|y, z) is a function of x and z;
p(y|x, z) g(y, z), i.e., p(y|x, z) is a function of y and z;
X and Y are conditionally independent given Z.


Part a
\[\begin{align*}
p(x|y, z) &= \frac{p(x, y, z)}{p(y)p(z)}\\
\implies p(x|y, z) &\propto p(x, y, z)\\
\implies p(x|y, z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Note that the only part of this that depends on X is \(f(x, z)\), which implies that \(p(x|y, z) \propto f(x, z)\).



Part b

Let’s solve this in the exact same way.

\[\begin{align*}
p(y|x, z) &= \frac{p(x, y, z)}{p(x)p(z)}\\
\implies p(y|x, z) &\propto p(x, y, z)\\
\implies p(y|x, z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Similarly, the only portion of \(f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\) that depends on y is the term \(g(y, z)\). Thus, \(p(y|x, z) \propto g(y, z)\).



Part c

To be conditionally independent, we need to show that \(p(x, y|z) \propto p(x|z)p(y|z)\).
Let’s begin with the same approach that we followed in parts a and b. We’ll obviously need to get a little fancier for this part, but let’s first show that $p(x, y|z) f(x,z)g(y,z):

\[\begin{align*}
p(y, x| z) &= \frac{p(x, y, z)}{p(z)}\\
\implies p(y,x| z) &\propto p(x, y, z)\\
\implies p(y,x| z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)h(z)\\
\implies p(y,x| z) &\propto f(x, z)g(y, z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Next, we need to think about \(p(x|z)\) and \(p(y|z)\).

\[\begin{align*}
p(x|z) &= \frac{p(x,z)}{p(z)}\\
p(x,z) \propto f(x,z)f(z)\\
\implies p(x|z)\propto f(x,z)\\
p(y|z) &= \frac{p(y,z)}{p(z)}\\
p(y,z) \propto g(y,z)f(z)\\
\implies p(y|z)\propto g(y,z)\\
\end{align*}\]

Combining these results, we see that \(p(x, y | z)\propto f(x,z)g(y,z)\implies p(x, y |z) \propto p(x|z)p(y|z)\). Thus, x and y are conditionally independent.

Part 5
PH 3.1

Part a
Assume Y1, . . . , Y100 are, conditional on θ, i.i.d. binary random variables with expectation θ. Write down the joint distribution of Pr(Y1 = y1, . . . , Y100 = y100|θ) in a compact form. Also write down the form of \(Pr(\sum PYi = y|θ)\).
\[\begin{align*}
f(y_1, ..., y_{100}|\theta) &= \prod_{i=1}^{100}f(y_i|\theta)\\
&= \theta^{\sum_{i = 1}^{100}y_i}(1 - \theta)^{n - \sum_{i = 1}^{100}y_i}\\
P\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{100}Y = y_i|\theta\right) &= {n \choose \sum y_i} \theta^{\sum y_i}(1 - \theta)^{n - \sum y_i}
\end{align*}\]


Part b
For the moment, suppose you believed that θ ∈ {0.0, 0.1, . . . , 0.9, 1.0}. Given that the results of the survey were \(\sum Yi = 57\), compute \(Pr(\sum Yi = 57|θ)\) for each of these 11 values of θ and plot these probabilities as a function of θ.

###################################### R ######################################
library(ggplot2)

# Define a function that will spit out the probability we're interested in
# computing
p_y_theta <- function(theta, n, y) {
    # y: a sum of bernouli trials
    # theta: a vector of values between 0 and 1 (can be length 1)
    # n: number of bernouli trials
    return(choose(n, y) * theta**y * (1 - theta)**(n - y))
}

# Define our primary input values (theta) and other given values (n, y)
theta <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 11)
n <- 100
y <- 57

# Figure out where the highest probability lies
max_prob_theta <- theta[
    which(p_y_theta(theta, n, y) == max(p_y_theta(theta, n, y)))
]
# Plot the outputs as nice and pretty as possible
plot_data <- data.frame(theta = theta, y = p_y_theta(theta, n, y))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = theta, y = y)) +
    geom_point(col = "skyblue", size = 2) +
    geom_line(col = "skyblue", lwd = 0.5, lty = 2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = max_prob_theta, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1, lty = 2) +
    labs(title = "Pr(sum(Y) = 57 | theta)", x = "Theta", y = "Probability") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        text = element_text(family = "serif"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
    )







###############################################################################


The plot shows a maximum at 0.6.



Part c
Now suppose you originally had no prior information to believe one of these θ-values over another, and so Pr(θ = 0.0) = Pr(θ = 0.1) = · · · = Pr(θ = 0.9) = Pr(θ = 1.0). Use Bayes’ rule to compute \(p(θ| \sum Yi = 57)\) for each θ-value. Make a plot of this posterior distribution as a function of θ.

I want to note that I used generative AI to assist me with the following code for this problem. I derived the the math to implement, and ChatGPT assisted with the coding:


###################################### R ######################################

# Define the function to compute posterior probability using Bayes' theorem
p_theta_bayes <- function(theta, n, y) {
    # Compute P(Y = 57 | θ) for each θ
    likelihood <- choose(n, y) * theta^y * (1 - theta)^(n - y)

    # Prior probabilities (uniform over 11 values)
    prior <- rep(1 / length(theta), length(theta))

    # Compute P(Y = 57) as the sum of likelihood * prior over all θ
    p_y <- sum(likelihood * prior)

    # Compute posterior using Bayes' rule
    posterior <- (likelihood * prior) / p_y

    return(posterior)
}

# Define theta values and known values of n and y
theta <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 11)
n <- 100
y <- 57

# Compute the posterior probabilities
posterior_probs <- p_theta_bayes(theta, n, y)

# Plot the posterior distribution
plot_data <- data.frame(theta = theta, posterior = posterior_probs)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = theta, y = posterior)) +
    geom_point(col = "blue", size = 2) +
    geom_line(col = "blue", lwd = 0.5, lty = 2) +
    labs(
        title = "Posterior Probability Distribution P(θ | Y = 57)",
        x = "Theta", y = "Posterior Probability"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        text = element_text(family = "serif"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
    )







###############################################################################



Part d
Now suppose you allow θ to be any value in the interval [0, 1]. Using the uniform prior density for θ, so that p(θ) = 1, plot the posterior density \(p(θ) × Pr(\sum Yi = 57|θ)\) as a function of θ.

###################################### R ######################################
library(ggplot2)

# Define function to compute posterior density
posterior_density <- function(theta_vals, n, y) {
    # Compute likelihood P(Y = 57 | θ)
    likelihood <- choose(n, y) * theta_vals^y * (1 - theta_vals)^(n - y)

    # Since prior is uniform (1), posterior is proportional to likelihood
    posterior <- likelihood

    return(posterior)
}

# Define a continuous range of theta values
theta_vals <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000) # More points for smooth curve
n <- 100
y <- 57

# Compute posterior density
posterior_vals <- posterior_density(theta_vals, n, y)

# Normalize for better visualization (optional, but makes y-axis interpretable)
posterior_vals <- posterior_vals / max(posterior_vals)

# Plot the posterior density
plot_data <- data.frame(theta = theta_vals, posterior = posterior_vals)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = theta, y = posterior)) +
    geom_line(col = "skyblue", lwd = 1) +
    labs(
        title = "Posterior Density p(θ | Y = 57)",
        x = "Theta", y = "Density (unnormalized)"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        text = element_text(family = "serif"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
    )
